headline: Widest thermal edge of the season fires up yellowfin on the Hudson's 100-fathom line
subhead: A mid-week blow sharpened the shelf-slope break to a 10-degree differential, and the tuna know it — here's where to find the seam and what's biting on it.
body_markdown:
Last week's blow did what a good blow always does out here — it made a mess for two days and then handed us the best structural setup we've seen all season. Southwest wind pushed hard Sunday into Monday, kicked up a sloppy 4-6 foot sea on the shelf, and for a minute it looked like a lost week. But underneath that chop, the wind was doing real work — piling warm slope water up against the cooler shelf water and sharpening the edge between them instead of blending it out. By Tuesday the differential across that break hit roughly 10.3°F, shelf to slope, which is the widest thermal wall I've measured all year. That's not a subtle gradient — that's a line you could practically draw with a ruler on the chartplotter, and it's sitting right where it should: along the shelf-slope transition east of the Hudson's main channel, from around Wilmington-Poor Man's over toward the canyon's east wall.

That edge is why Wednesday and Thursday of this week are the window I'd circle if I could only pick two days. Seas are settling behind the blow, the seam is holding rather than sliding, and yellowfin have already found it. The moon is working in our favor too — we're waning down toward the new moon around the middle of the month, which means darker nights building through the week. That matters more than people think out here, because darker skies mean the squid-light bite at night gets better fish reaction, less moon glow washing out the underwater lights. Combine that with a sharpening 20 to 30 fathom break from the NE upwelling and you've got a legitimate two-species week — yellowfin in the canyon by day, bluefin on the inside grounds after dark.

We worked the Wilmington-Poor Man's seam Tuesday and had a mixed morning turn into a strong afternoon once we found where the color changed from that dirty green shelf water into the cleaner blue slope push. Yellowfin from 45 to about 70 pounds came on a standard spread — naked ballyhoo on the long riggers, a green machine and a small Ilander/ballyhoo combo down the shotgun, cedar plugs in close on the flat lines. Nothing fancy, but the fish were sitting right on that thermal wall and once we located it the bite stayed consistent for a solid three-hour stretch on the troll. The east wall of the Hudson itself, out past the Dip, produced smaller class fish mixed with a couple of bigeye-looking marks on the sounder that we couldn't get to eat — worth a jig drop if you've got the crew for it, but I wouldn't plan a trip around it yet.

The real story for the back half of the week might be the bluefin, not the yellowfin. The Coimbra corridor — that 20-fathom stretch on the inside edge of the canyon grounds — is holding a legitimate concentration of school-to-mid-size bluefin, and the NE upwelling sharpening that break is stacking bait right where the fish want it. With the moon darkening through the week, this is squid-light water at night: get anchored or drifting over the break after dark, lights down, and let the squid show up on their own schedule. We've seen 40 to 70-pound class bluefin working those bait balls consistently, and jigging into marks with a Shimano Butterfly-style jig or a smaller vertical iron has been more efficient than trying to troll them up in the dark. If you're not a night owl, working that same stretch at first light with a small spread of cedar plugs and green machines has still produced a fish or two before the sun gets high.

Mahi have been a bonus rather than a target this week — a few gaffers in the 8 to 15 pound range came off scattered weed patches on the troll near the seam, nothing concentrated enough to call a pattern yet. No real wahoo activity to report, and I'd be lying if I told you there was — the water's warm enough for them but we haven't seen the high-speed strikes that usually tip us off. White marlin is the one everybody's asking about, and the honest answer is: not yet. The warm plume that needs to push up onto the bank hasn't fully arrived — we're looking at a 7 to 10 day window before that trigger sets up properly at the mid-Atlantic canyons, the Hudson included. I wouldn't build a trip around marlin this week, but I'd have the pitch bait rigged just in case, because when that plume shows up it tends to show up fast.

If I had one day this week, I'd take Wednesday or Thursday, run straight for the Wilmington-Poor Man's seam first, and work the color change hard before shifting east toward the Dip if the bite softens. If the crew can handle a night trip, Friday into Saturday at Coimbra under lights is the play for bluefin, especially with the moon continuing to darken. Either way, this is a week to trust the thermal break over any single set of coordinates — that 10-degree wall is going to move a little day to day, and the fish are going to move with it. Find the edge, don't fish the spot.
